definition: Lexicographic max-min optimization (also called lexmaxmin or leximin or leximax or lexicographic max-ordering optimization) is a kind of multi-objective optimization.
details: In general, multi-objective optimization deals with optimization problems with two or more objective functions to be optimized simultaneously. Lexmaxmin optimization presumes that the decision-maker would like the smallest objective value to be as high as possible; subject to this, the second-smallest objective should be as high as possible; and so on. In other words, the decision-maker ranks the possible solutions according to a leximin order of their objective function values. As an example, consider egalitarian social planners, who want to decide on a policy such that the utility of the poorest person will be as high as possible; subject to this, they want to maximize the utility of the second-poorest person; and so on. This planner solves a lexmaxmin problem, where the objective function number i is the utility of agent number i. Algorithms for lexmaxmin optimization (not using this name) were developed for computing the nucleolus of a cooperative game. An early application of lexmaxmin was presented by Melvin Dresher in his book on game theory, in the context of taking maximum advantage of the opponent's mistakes in a zero-sum game. Behringer cites many other examples in game theory as well as decision theory.

explainer.lead: Lexmaxmin is a multi-objective optimisation in which the decision-maker first maximises the smallest objective, then the second-smallest, and so on. It matters when fairness among objectives matters more than total sum.

tiers.eli5: Like making sure the worst-off person is as well off as possible before you start improving anyone else.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it to allocate resources so no single objective is starved, solving a sequence of max-min subproblems. A pitfall is the cost of repeated solves and sensitivity to how ties in the smallest values are broken.
tiers.paperLevel: Ranks solutions by leximin order on their objective vectors: maximise the smallest objective value, subject to that maximise the second-smallest, and so on. Known limits include computational expense from the sequence of constrained optimisations.

explainer.example: With three objectives yielding vectors (2,5,9) and (3,3,4), lexmaxmin prefers the second because its smallest value, 3, exceeds 2.
